title: hyperlinks | incertae sedis
description: the digital presence of (dubiously) "creative type" "incertae sedis"
text: hyperlinks | incertae sedis music doodles photos links etc THE BEST OF THE WWW (some stuff I like) Please check out my associate's site here: Here are some other personal sites I like (and for which I can find buttons), most also hosted on Neocities: (All Neocities sites I follow) Resources and tools Preface: Free and open source software rundown I don't have much to say about these except that they work, and that some of them work very well. Many are the default or most famous choice for their respective uses, but if you're new to FOSS or trying to do something unfamiliar you might not have heard of them, so here you go. Blender - 3D Graphics (the only one on this list I have not touched myself, I fear) Audacity - Audio editor (basic) LMMS - Digital Audio Workstation (somewhat less basic, electronic music-focused) Sound Juicer - CD Ripper Foliate - eBook reader FontForge - Font editor GNU Image Manipulation Program - Image editor, raster Inkscape - Image editor, vector VLC - Media player MKVToolNix - .mkv/Matroska editor Lollypop - Music player (clean and "i have all my stuff on a pretty virtual shelf"-core) Strawberry - Music player (busy and "i fucking love metadata"-core) LibreOffice - Office suite Ubuntu Linux - Operating system (yeah I'm as normie as they come) MuseScore - Scorewriter OBS Studio - Screen recorder and streaming JPEXS Free Flash Decompiler - SWF Decompiler Swivel - SWF to Video Converter (note: crashed when attempting to combine uncompressed video and audio) Kdenlive - Video editor Mozilla Firefox - Web broswer Wine - Windows compatibility layer for Linux yt-dlp - Web video downloader (command-line) FFMpeg Literally one of the most important software libraries ever, half the software that plays or processes video uses it. Includes encoders and decoders for both open-source formats and reverse-engineered proprietary ones (at least in some builds). It is a command-line tool and kind of imposing, so here's a guide to a bunch of common tasks. Internet Archive One of the Internet's twin pillars of knowledge, in my opinion. Famous for the Wayback Machine, a fairly wide and deep set of snapshots of the whole public Web, containing many treasures otherwise lost. Aside from this, it is a digital library with many collections to its name, some digitized or compiled by its own efforts and some mirrors. Also allows anyone to make an account and upload, so hosts a heck of a lot of other media (with very little apparent moderation so be warned about browsing without a set goal.) MakeMKV I don't know what this is doing here. Hyperlink. I don't know what that's doing there either. Definitely do not click that one. More seriously though, MakeMKV is an optical disc ripper (not open-source). Making copies of media you own for personal "space-shifting" use is legal in the US and some kind of grey area in a lot of other places. If doing so requires breaking encryption then you might be breaking a law anywhere though. Obviously don't break any laws, everyone knows laws always serve your interests and not just those of some kind of "privileged economic class" MDN Web Docs Extremely comprehensive documentation for HTML, CSS, and JS, always written to the level of detail needed to actually follow what things do (and often with demonstrations.) Ruffle An emulator for Flash media, available both as a browser extension and as a library that can be used directly in webpages. It does not support every feature of newer versions of Flash but is getting close, so most SWF files will mostly work. uBlock Origin An adblocker (and a general content blocker for anything malicious or annoying). It's probably the most popular blocker out there, so the blocklists it uses are actively maintained. Most effective on Firefox, and a bit less effective on Chrome due to some recent API modifications. W3Schools Slightly less comprehensive HTML, CSS, and JS reference than the MDN docs, but covers every commonly used feature, has beginner-friendly tutorials, and is a reference for a bunch of other web technologies and programming languages! Wikimedia Foundation The Internet's other twin pillar of knowledge, most known for Wikipedia. The average person knows what Wikipedia is, but maybe not their other projects like Wikimedia Commons (open-licensed image and media repository) or Wiktionary (comprehensive multilingual dictionary, complete with etymology and usage examples), both of which I consult fairly regularly. Web comics All Night Laundry Begun on the MSPA forums, this story quickly reached a level of plot and mechanic complexity greater even than that of Homestuck. Kind of reminiscent of Matt Smith era Dr Who (meant in the good way.) Instantly root-for-able protagonist, excellent horror, dodgy but conceptually fascinating science. Dialogue is a bit jank once the story gains more characters but it was written on a forum ok Dinosaur Comics Fixed-art comic using premade dinosaur graphics that apparently gave Ryan North's computer a virus when he downloaded them. Aside from the occasional story arc or running gag, serves as a staging ground for the author's random thoughts. Drive This comic doesn't have an RSS feed and now I've forgotten to read it and I have no idea what's going on!! Ahhh!!! Pretty good science fiction story. Unwinnable wars... technological thefts... missing identity... UPDATE: This User Has Found The RSS Feed Dr. McNinja Somehow makes "random equals funny" and "smashing together badass things makes a more badass thing" work. A serious contender for the title of greatest web comic of all time. Occasionally the comedy is overly edgy and grating near the start of the comic but this gets ironed out. Gang Fight ok I haven't read many of the comics here yet but look at this freakin website! Look at it!!! Gunnerkrigg Court Magic school story (uh, science school, rather) where the school is not all that it seems... known for its beginnings as a slice-of-life blended with a longer-form epic plot, the plot has tipped more into epic these days. Kid Radd (archive by Brad Greco) Sprite comic with then-unusual animated elements. Very silly and early 2000s but turns surprisingly philosophical by the end. MS Paint Adventures *sigh* yeah i'm a homestuck. the first two ms paint adventures are dumb and probably not worth reading. Problem Sleuth is a lil edgy but very much worth reading. Homestuck will likely poison your mind for life. It's simultaneously one of the most artistically important web comics ever made and flawed enough to make many readers bootstrap the entire structure of media criticism while thinking about it. It's hilarious, poignant, epic, and medium-breaking, but dare I say... problematic... Pokey the Penguin Fun in the Arctic Circle with Pokey and friends! Sometimes hard to understand! Secret Knots, The Haunting one-off comics by Juan Santapau. I mean if you describe the premise of half of these they just sound goofy but no, they're more haunting. smbc Funnier than XKCD Weirdly preoccupied with robots exterminating humanity, though. Spacetrawler Straddles the line between gag-a-day and space opera. Nowadays not quite as elegant in doing so but still worth checking out, and the original arc is great in the way of concept, humor and character. tisTree Seasonal stories featuring fully characterized GeoCities gifs, including the titular tisTree. As a love letter to GeoCities-era creativity, Taras Tymoshenko appears to have built the whole project using a fairly old-fashioned HTML edifice. Wondermark Notable for being composited from old (turn of the 19th century) line illustrations. Infrequently updated nowadays. xkcd It's the classic geek webcomic. Some people knock XKCD for being relatively unfunny, "too reddit," etc but it's charming and indisputably a good source of digestible infographics. Also the "What If?" pages completely live up to the promise of their concept. Web non-comics (moving pictures) Alan Resnick Eerie and amusing performance art, 3D animation and comedy sketches and horror shorts, often speculative-technological. Baman Piderman While the name would suggest this is a superhero parody series, Baman and Piderman share no features with their namesakes besides appearance. The cast quickly grew beyond these two and also are the cutest bunch imaginable. Usually visually minimal, but expressively animated, and characters' bodies often are seen disobey laws of anatomy and physics. Carter Amelia Davis Fever dreams you'd have falling asleep at the computer circa 2009. Cyriak Harris If you were on YouTube as a kid Cyriak's initially innocent body-horror animation loops may have either traumatized or fascinated you. Luckily I was in the latter category. Most original videos are synchronized to his dissonant, poppy electronic tracks. Diminish Will (fictional) is tasked with completing the platformer his sister made for him before her death. Tone bounces between a high-energy twitch stream and a nearly unfiltered exploration of grief. Homestar Runner Central to much of 2000s online culture. Weird Flash animated comedy sketches in the town of Free Country USA, with a population rarely visibly exceeding a dozen. You will never forget these characters. Illusion Lock Begins as a Petscop-inspired game development log, ends as a machinima puppet show character drama and a growing mythology. The series might be over or there might be a new storyline in the works, it's been unexpectedly revived several times. Local 58 TV The Analog horror O G, introducing what are now worn tropes with an untarnished gravity. Petscop The story of Paul and the unfinished PS1 game he found. The game and his life are full of compounding mysteries, many answers we are never privy to. Pretty much nothing else feels like watching this. Pilotredsun A main progenitor of surreal, deliberately error-laden animation on YouTube. Visually evolves from MS Paint-core to something a 90s alt cartoon to writhing digital painting. Also makes excellent music under the names PilotRedSun and PilotRedSky. ratboygenius Mixed-digital-media children's series that teaches the values of ??? ??? and often terrifies stragglers. Beautiful soundtracks. Possibly indoctrination into a metaphysical system of world-as-dream. Stockroach OFFICIAL, The STOCK-A-DOODLE-DOO, MONEYGRUBS. A beautiful tale told through screen recordings of the recovery and coming-of-age of a definitely-late-30s business man. To be clear this isn't actually a financial advice channel (well, The Stockroach attempts to make it such but is usually distracted by his creative talents and personal troubles). Technology Connections A guy named Alec who is extremely enthusiastic about how technologies work, from the omnipresent to the obsolete and obscure, and always succeeds at sharing that enthusiasm. Also has killer scripts, delivery, and recording setups. Only nonfiction in this section so far, oops Worthikids A master of two particular forms of Blender animation: photorealistic stop-motion and 2D composite. Beyond looking gorgeous, his animations are usually of the living-vicariously-through-hilarious-strangers'-relationships comedy type and i live on that stuff. Writing 17776 & 20020 Jon Bois' projections of what football will be like in the future. Beloved and unexpected narrators. 70s SciFi Art (Adam Rowe) Posts about trends in science fiction artwork of the 1970s (or in the same stylistic traditions), often meaning extremely specific recurring elements. Scans are of course featured. Rowe has created an artbook on the subject, Worlds Beyond Time , as well. ctrlcreep Evocative fantasist working with a dizzying array of speculative-fiction concepts. A writer of microfiction, famously, and also longer works. Jennifer Mills News Usually-weekly online newspaper entirely about trivial events in the life of one Jennifer Mills, running since long before the invention of microblogging. Something about the objective reporter tone contrasted with headlines like "Woman Wears Hat" never gets old for me, I dunno. Each issue also features a Poetry Corner with at least two brief and pleasant works of doggerel. late review, the (Kate Wagner) Simultaneously hyperliterate and inviting essays covering both topical subjects and personal fascinations, including, of course, architecture (Wagner is best known for McMansion Hell , a blog that helps you find new ways to laugh at bad design decisions and really sells the horror of wealth inequality.) She is also on Neocities Pluralistic (Cory Doctorow) Usually-daily blog covering current events and the history leading to them, usually regarding digital freedom and tech policy (what Doctorow has been know for forever, both in his nonfiction and fiction). Also always features interesting links, and often features reviews of recommended new books. One complaint I have is that Doctorow tends to frequently repeat very similar points in very similar language, but at least he's always stating it well. SCP Foundation What began as one short bureaucratic horror piece has become one of the largest creative writing communities on the Web, growing into numerous horror and speculative fiction genres, some of which have reached entirely new depths of expression here. Personal / Portfolio / Misc / Categories are hard Alice Averlong Wiki Alice Averlong is a retrotech enthusiast and well experienced in both retrotech archival and retrotech "Shenanigans". On this wiki you'll find links to a bunch of stuff she's made and to social media threads on various topics (invariably meandering and entertaining). Possibly best known for creating the Death Generator, which creates facsimile dialog boxes for dozens of retro games. brian david gilbert Apparently biding his time until he can either break into television or become a rural shopkeep. Brian David Gilbert became recognized for his short musical comedy videos. He continues to create the occasional musical comedy video, though usually less frivolous than of old. Also has put out some excellent horror shorts (not intentionally a jorts joke). Conway's Game of Life (implementation by Fabian/copy) Darn fast implementation. The user can load many famous and interesting patterns, from humble still lifes to a full Turing machine. For those unaware of what the Game of Life is: here's the rules: there's a grid of square tiles that can either be "dead" or alive". At each step, cells with three neighbors come to life and cells with zero or more than three neighbors die. Music Animation Machine If you've ever watched a classical music video on YouTube you've at least seen the thumbnails of musanim's color-coded piano roll videos. Channel creator Stephen Malinowski has been developing this or precursor software since the 1980s and has created thousands of videos in the last two decades, often testing new visualization methods and emphases. There might be a downloadable version somewhere. Neil Cicierega Sometimes regarded as the secret mastermind behind all that was good and hilarious during early Web 2.0. At any rate created or co-created a prodigious amount of comedy, horror comedy, meme, meme comedy, meme horror, and meme horror comedy work, a good deal of which has either aged well or has become a beautiful time capsule. Also he is Lemon Demon, an excellent synth-rock act. Runouw Runouw are brothers Robert and Steven Hewitt (but mostly Robert?) and they made some of the greatest Flash games of all time. The most famous is Super Mari o 63, but their originals ought to be equally iconic. Especially the Last Legacy games- get you a flash emulator and check them out pronto! seximal.net SFW, I promise. Advocacy and a naming system for Base 6 numbers, and various other resources and systematizations of a similar nature. Suricrasia Online Shark ISP. Demoscene artist and unfictionalist. Silicon Zoo, The Micrographs of drawings hidden by silicon chip designers! It's two of my favorite things: niche artistic traditions, and niche artistic tradition archival. Mystery Flesh Pit What if the National Park Service used to maintain trails inside a buried Old God? What could possibly have gone wrong? TARDIS Builders A forum dedicated to Doctor Who prop references, plans, models, and builds, especially the TARDIS exterior and interior (i am fixated on the latter). Not as active as it was before its months offline but still a great resource. T-Bug "All: We are the men men men" Wendy Carlos One of the pioneers of the 60s wave of synthesizer music, she created the best-selling "Switched-on Bach" on the Moog and several famous film scores. She later produced innovative works in digital sound synthesis and alternative tuning. Her website details these and other interests and projects, and provides downloadable resources for many. It also remains firmly in the mid-Web 1.0 design tradition, both visually and in its occasional references to the novelty of Web technology. Sitemap FAQ thank you for visiting my web site! :-)

title: DMANS WEB - FILM REVIEWS
text: DMANS WEB - FILM REVIEWS DMANS WEB Say Anything (8/7/26) Disclosure Day (8/4/26) Kill Bill: The Whole Bloody Affair (5/29/26) It Was Just an Accident (5/29/26) Avatar: Fire and Ash (1/26/26) Mad Max Beyond Thunderdome (11/17/25) Tron: Ares (10/16/25) Relay (9/22/25) The Raid (9/22/25) Formula 1 Movie (7/16/25) The Phoenician Scheme (6/20/25) Sinners (5/6/25) Mickey 17 (5/6/25) Past Lives (3/15/25) Roman Holiday (3/3/25) The Brutalist (3/3/25) Flow (1/5/25) Anora (11/17/24) Lawrence of Arabia (11/13/24) Indiana Jones Trilogy (8/20/24) Casablanca (8/13/24) Memories of Murder (8/8/24) Furiosa (6/17/24) Challengers (5/30/24) Godzilla: Minus One (5/30/24) Monkey Man The Holdovers Dune: Part Two Io Capitano SAY ANYTHING I came for the boombox scene, but stayed for a wholesome, sincere and irresistibly positive rom-com. Say Anything is a film from another era proving that not all Hollywood romances were toxic in those days. Lloyd Dobler is a guy that most guys can aspire to be and most women can aspire to be with. Polite and respectful, but also confident and driven. I feel you rarely see a man pour his heart out and dedicate his life to a girl without it coming off as creepy or desperate. Lloyd Dobler is never desperate, he just decided to take a chance on a girl he likes. The reason it worked? Well if we look at the remarks Diane makes during this movie about Lloyd it becomes clear: He makes her laugh, he looks out for her and perhaps most important, when she is with him she feels like she doesn't have to act a certain way. He makes her feel completely at ease with herself. Say Anything is filled with memorable scenes and characters. Even characters that only get a few seconds of screentime have souls, which is not an easy feat to pull of. I love how the story outline is incredibly standard and predictable, but the script cleverly avoids so many clichÃ©s it could have fallen for. Diane's dad is against their relationship, but he doesn't try to stop her from seeing him outright. He wants her to come to the conclusion herself that their relationship is bad for her which is probably what most clever dads would do. I also think Lloyd's female friends are great, trying to be supportive but meanwhile having their own insecurities to deal with, much like actual friends. In the end, the boombox scene was almost underwhelming (but not really, its a great moment) for how short it was and how it didn't straight up resolve the breakup like I expected it to. The thing is, Say Anything is filled to the brim with wholesome, and memorable scenes making the boombox scene just one of many. The scene where Lloyd tries to hang out with 'the guys' after breakup was incredibly powerful and I feel should become required watching material for insecure teenage boys who are edging towards the manosphere. If those so called studs know so much about women, how come they're sitting in front of a gas station drinking beer on a saturday night? I don't really do ratings or stars but in terms of romantic comedy films it doesn't get much better than Say Anything. I will now go off on a voyage to watch more Cameron Crowe and John Cusack films, bye! DISCLOSURE DAY Disclosure Day, supposedly, was the first blockbuster film by Steven Spielberg in a very long time. It had a lot of buzz going, but ultimately led fans feeling dissappointed. I even read reviews and comments saying Spielberg needs to stop making action movies and whatnot. So let me just give you my two cents on this film and Spielberg's career at this point. First of all, I love Spielberg both as a director and as a personality in Hollywood. I don't think everybody quite appreciates how much he has shaped the film industry, for better and for worse. Spielberg single handedly introduced the summer blockbuster concept with Jaws and directed several film franchises that are (unfortunately) still ongoing. Spielberg has also got producer credits on Back to the Future, Gremlins, Poltergeist, Shrek, Twister, The Flintstones (as Steven Spielrock) and even Small Soldiers. As such, I believe nobody should have the audacity to say that Spielberg should just stop making action movies. He has earned the credit to make that decision for himself. This all being said, I do understand the dissappointment a lot of people felt after having seen Disclosure Day. Some of it can be attributed to mismarketing. Disclosure Day is actually a lot more about people than it is about aliens. It raises the question if our civilization could handle the truth if it turned out that aliens existed and were seeking contact with humans. I actually enjoyed this ongoing debate throughout the film and surely there is no right answer, because we have no idea how the world would react to such a revelation. This aspect made it ambiguous for me who the real villains were supposed to be in this film. Looking back I did enjoy the acting performances, although they were a bit over the top here and there. I saw a side of Emily Blunt and Colin Firth I haven't seen before. The action scenes though, were wonky and outdated. I completely agree with this criticism. The action scenes in Disclosure Day would have worked a lot better 30 to 40 years ago. Times have simply changed. Directors like Nolan, Villeneuve and Marvel Studios have raised the bar as to what blockbuster movies are supposed to look like. Sure you can argue that Spielberg has done a lot better with projects like Jurassic Park and Saving Private Ryan, but still I think Disclosure Day would have been received better in a bygone era. Disclosure Day is a film made in 2026 with an 80s mindset. Like all Spielberg movies, its centered on human drama over excessive action and CGI spectacle and unfortunately this is not the industry standard anymore. The scene where the whole gang turns invisible and hurries off in an invisible firetruck to a film studio in order to broadcast the truth is very quirky, but would have worked fine in a film like ET or Close Encounters. So while I could never say to Spielberg that it's time to call it quits on action movies, I'm sure that Disclosure Day was a learning experience for him as well of how the film landscape has changed, for better and for worse. KILL BILL: THE WHOLE BLOODY AFFAIR When Kill Bill came around in two parts in 2003 and 2004 I was just a bit too young to be able to watch it in the theatres. I remember being upset about the film being cut in half, because Tarantino wanted it to be a magnificent 4 hour epic. I bought both films on DVD when they came out and while I very much enjoyed both halves, I thought the movies were out of balance. Part One leaned much more into samurai sword violence, whereas part two was slower, with more introspection and a finale that completely subverted my expectations. Yesterday I had the opportunity to finally watch "The Whole Bloody Affair" in my local cinema. In glorious 70mm analogue film, with the extented O-Ren anime sequence, the omission of the cliffhanger at the end of Part One and the addition of a (very weird) animated Fortnite post-credit scene directed by Tarantino. Some things I noticed when watching this: 1. Holy shit this film has stood the test of time really well! Kill Bill looks flawless 23 years after release. Every scene is eye candy. The fight scenes are gorgeous, but also ridiculously over the top. The House of Blue Leaves fight scene is very, very long but changes pace and setting often enough to not become repetitive. Also, kudos to so many strong female characters without ever getting preachy about it! 2. The omission of the cliffhanger at the end of Part One changes the viewing experience a LOT! To be honest, I forgot about this twist and when it finally landed after 3.5 hours I was just as speechless as The Bride. You feel the earth shattering under your feet and for a few minutes everything you saw until then stops making sense. 3.This almost goes without saying, but Kill Bill really works a lot better as a single film. By going straight into part two after the House of Blue Leaves, you are given a necessary break from the overwhelming, mind numbing action and gore. As you learn more about The Bride and Bill, the film gains emotional depth. So instead of having one action packed first half versus a more introspective second half, you have one complete, balanced film and the directoral choices make a lot more sense this way. 4. The animated Fortnite sequence meant nothing to me. It felt very much out of place and I get that it was a scene that Tarantino wanted in the film from first, but after 23 years it is just too late to make new additions. Also I did not care for the video game animation style. 5. Last but not least, I freakin miss Michael Madsen! What a bad ass! IT WAS JUST AN ACCIDENT This Iranian film directed by Jafar Panahi got all the praise in the last award season, walking away with a Palme d'Or even. I was intrigued by the premise of this film and sure enough, It Was Just An Accident has an excellent starting point putting you at the edge of your seat. A man working at a garage believes to have found the guard who tortured him when he walks into his shop with car trouble. He knocks him out, but before he takes his revenge he wants a second opinion to identify the guard. Unfortunately, very little is done to intricate the story. What follows is the assembly of a band of trauma survivors who then spend the better part of an hour driving around with their supposed guard knocked out in their truck, arguing about the morality of vengeance and exposing their traumata one by one. The endless bickering seemed entirely pointless and did nothing but stretch the duration of what should have been a short film into a feature filn. Towards the end, when the supposed guard is finally faced, a heavy but quite predictable dialogue unfolds about how everybody is really a victim in a totalitarian regime like Iran. The final scene was dark and depressing in a very good way, but by then I was already tuned out too much for it to land properly. If this movie was somewhere between 30-45 minutes it would have worked a lot better, but alas. AVATAR: FIRE AND ASH When the first Avatar movie came out in 2009 I was blown away by the visual spectacle. The story was nothing we hadn't seen before, but it was a gorgeous movie to watch. One of the few that didn't use 3D as a gimmick but rather to create depth and immersion. The first Avatar became a smash hit, with James Cameron dethroning his very own Titanic as the highest grossing film of all time. Then, we had to wait 14 freakin' years for a sequel. The Way of Water performed great financially, but it did not outperform the original. If you look at film franchises in the 21st century, like The Dark Knight trilogy or the Avengers movies, you see that sequels usually perform better than the original. The fact that Way of Water did not, to me was a telltale sign. The Avatar franchise had lost its momentum. As we speak, Fire and Ash is ranking at the 19th place in the box office, which can only be considered a disappointment. I went to watch Fire and Ash as intended. In 3D and with a high frame rate. I don't consider myself a fan of the franchise, but always go out to see them. The Avatar movies to me are the ultimate form of escapism. No other movie allows me to be immersed in another world so deeply and completely. What I love the most about these movies is just exploring the planet Pandora. All the different na'vi tribes, creatures and biomes. In that regard, Fire and Ash was certainly a bit of a let down. While we did get to meet some new tribes, most of the film was set, once again, in the water biome of the prevous film. I really liked the banshee tribe and its antagonistic leader and I think the third act of the movie should have been relocated to their volcanic world somehow to keep things fresh. While this for me is a significant point of criticism, I still enjoyed Fire and Ash very much. Sully's extended family is starting to grow on me, especially Kira and Spider are interesting characters. For future films I hope that Cameron will choose another protagonist like Spider or one of Sully's children. I hope that we will continue exploring this wonderful CGI world that James Cameron created with his studio. The Avatar movies are without a doubt the most beautiful CGI films ever made. All the time and effort put into making these movies should be enough for anyone to go see them in the theatre. MAD MAX BEYOND THUNDERDOME Over the years I have developed a habit of not caring what other people think about a movie. I try to avoid movie trailers and reading reviews until after I've seen a film. In fact, when there is a circlejerk of dislike for certain a movie I am even more inclined to watch it because usually it means there is something interesting going on. Mad Max Thunderdome is widely regarded as the lesser title in the franchise. Audience and critics reception were mixed and the film underformed financially. I think a lot of the disappointment comes from the big tonal shift compared to the first two Mad Max films. Watching Thunderdome, I couldn't help but think I was watching a story in the Star Wars universe. Thunderdome, in spite of its name, is much less violent than Road Warrior and its 21st century sequels. Max is still mostly a silent protagonist, but has more heart and empathy than before. Thunderdome also does a lot more world building than its predecessors, which is an enrichment for the franchise. Places like Bartertown and Planet Erf really speak to the imagination and they spared no expense in making these sets come to life. Also, for a movie that is considered a disappointment, it has surely left its footprint on the collective memory of the world. Terms like Thunderdome, Master Blaster and the phrase "Two Men Enter, One Man Leaves" all originate from here! Also don't forget the hit song "We Don't Need Another Hero" by Tina Turner which was made for this movie. Her appearance in this film is equally fascinating. Miller wrote her character with Tina in mind, not sure if she would be interested in playing it but she was! She did a fine job as Aunty, playing a villian who can be ruthless at times, but emphatic and forgiving as well. I guess that is the legacy of Thunderdome. It is by far the most humane, hopeful story in the Mad Max universe as it tries to imagine a world after the apocalypse. Do not skip this title when diving into the Mad Max franchise! TRON: ARES A very entertaining third installment in the Tron franchise that keeps on underperforming whilst building a sort of cult following at the same time. Ares looks to be heading towards the same fate judging from the very empty theater I sat in during opening weekend. I got the full Imax 3D experience and was very much entertained. While this Tron is probably the least innovative visually, building on the visual style created by Kosinski and the amazing score by Daft Punk from Legacy, this Tron does one thing right. It actually has a clear storyline. Moving the action into the real world was a good idea because the grid always seemed to be a rather empty place in previous films. The concept of 3D printed evil programs that evaporate after 29 minutes is a really cool plot device that creates a lot of the tension in this film. The story is easy enough to follow, allowing full immersion in the swell action scenes. To its credit, the action scenes Tron reminded me a bit of Terminator 2. The actors do not stand out very much but did an ok job. Leto actually did a fine job as a charismatic program. Since there isn't a lot of blockbuster competition in the theater at the moment I suggest you give Tron Ares a chance. Less innovative, but more entertaining than its 1982 and 2010 predecessors. RELAY If you are only going to watch one more film for the remainder of this year, let it be Relay. I enjoyed the hell out of this well paced, intelligent action film. When I was a teenager Tony Scott's Enemy of the State was my favorite movie and Relay certainly hits in the same ballpark in terms of story and atmosphere. The film is about whistle blowers who regret their whistle blowing, for instance because of being threatened and intimidated by their former companies, and are looking for a way out. This may sound pretty unheroic, but is probably closer to the truth than we would like to believe. Whistle blowing is an extremely important and courageous act, but whistle blowers are often not received as heroes by society. Riz Ahmed is the Gene Hackman of relay, who lives a reclusive life, helping other people to get their life back. Lily James is the next whistle blower in need of Ahmed's services. I thought both actors were a great cast. What Relay shows the audience without telling it, is that if you want to remain anonymous in the 21st century, outdated technology is the only way to go. Riz Ahmed is never seen behind a VPN, relying on the US Postal Service and the Tri-State Relay Service for people with disabilities to communicate with his cliÃ«nts instead. The many scenes with the main character interacting through the relay service was a fresh touch. Relay does a good job of building the tension, suprising the audience with some excellent twists and keeping me at the edge of my seat like I haven't been for quite some time. THE RAID After having been recommended this film for years by people I finally sat down to watch The Raid. It is said to be one of the best action movies from Asia, if not one of the best in general, so you can imagine my expectations were pretty high. What you will notice right away when watching The Raid is how this movie drops you straight into the action without any warming up. The plot, the main characters and the goals are all layed out in the first five minutes. I appreciated this a lot, because modern action movies just drag on for too long. This movie is all meat and no fat, spoiling the audience with almost non-stop action and fighting scenes. The Raid is both an exhibition and an homage to the Indonesian fighting style of Silat, meaning you will be spoiled with largely uncut fighting scenes. The choreography is amazing and the use of objects in the building to get rid of enemies is very inventive, creating some memorable kill shots. There are a few moments to take a breath, using the time so reveal interesting plot twists. The short runtime of The Raid prevents you from becoming fatigued from all the violence. I do think that Hollywood has largely forgotten how to make action movies that work, perhaps with the exception of the Mad Max franchise. What The Raid gets right is that action movies should never be too long, preferably under 2 hours, and should have a story that is easy to follow. When the story becomes too complex, it prevents the viewer from being able to fully be immersed in the action. The Raid was a delicious unhealthy snack for me and I am already craving for its sequel that fortunately exists. FORMULA 1 MOVIE In spite of how much I hate every movie nowadays being tied to known intellectual properties, I contradict myself every now and then by seeing a movie like Formula 1. I am hardly a fan of autosports but I felt confident that this film was going to be good because of the people behind it. Brad Pitt's film production company Plan B has produced a lot of interesting work so far and I am down for whatever they release. Autosport films have a pretty bad rep, but since Joseph Kosinski was able to make a ridiculously fun thrill ride out of Top Gun: Maverick, he looked like the right man for this job. On the whole I enjoyed the F1 film. The story is very, very formulaic, but the execution is solid. This film's main strengths are the casting and acting performances. I liked Javier Bardem and Damson Idris as the arrogant talented rookie. Kerry Condon also deserves praise for her role, I'd like to see more of her in the future. However, this film would be nothing without Brad Pitt. It's amazing how much charisma one person can pour into a movie. I went home thinking that even though this movie would probably never have been made without the financial backing of the real Formula 1, the film would be better if it did not rely so heavily on that IP. I did not care for Lewis Hamilton and Max Verstappen existing in this semi-fictional F1 universe. It distracts from the main characters. It also demotes the Formula 1 movie to a corporate propaganda piece. The biggest lie this movie tries to sell is that Formula 1 is fun. Try to watch an actual race and you will find it to be 1 lap of action followed by 55 laps of fast cars carrying on single file towards a finish line. I'm exaggerating, but once the race has begun most of the fun happens around pit stops and safety car situations. This is why you see so many of those in the movie. I would recommend the Formula 1 film as this year's action packed, Brad Pitt containing summer blockbuster. Just keep in mind that in spite of all the F1 propaganda being thrown at you, you're watching a very fictional story. THE PHOENICIAN SCHEME There was a time when Wes Anderson was high on my list of favorite filmmakers. His unique style, his dry sense of humour, the emotional detachment of his characters and the extraordinary attention to composition and details in each and every scene make him an artisan within the film industry. I loved works like The Royal Tenenbaums, The Darjeeling Limited and Moonrise Kingdom for the above mentionted qualities, but also because they were sincere works of art. Over the course of his career I believe Wes Anderson lost that sincerity in his work. The emotional detachment has been replaced by a complete absence of emotion. Anderson doubled down on his quirky, signature style and unfortunately became a charicature of himself. Actually, I did watch all his works since his acclaimed Grand Budapest Hotel. I found Isle of Dogs, The French Dispatch and Asteroid City all falling in the same category. Wonderful to look at, but otherwise shallow and forgettable. Like walking through a fairy tale village in a theme park. The Phoenician Scheme might actually be his most sincere and emotional work in a long time. This is in no small part due to the strong performances of Threapleton and Cera, both newcomers in the otherwise tight-knit Anderson clique and main actor Benicio Del Toro who only joined the club since The French Dispatch. Del Toro brings a lot of humanity to his character, reminiscent of Hackman's role in The Royal Tenenbaums, and does not conform too much to the "Anderson" style. Threapleton plays her character full of contradictions flawlessly. As for Cera, I was just happy to see him on the big screen again and I wondered why the hell he wasn't invited to an Anderson film sooner. He was made for this stuff. Although the story is meager and the compartmentalized story structure does take a lot of pacing out of the film, in the end The Phoenician Scheme turned out to be a more sincere, artistic work than everything else Anderson made in the last decade. SINNERS It's always a pleasure, but increasingly a rarity, to watch big budget Hollywood films not based on any known intellectual property. Studios are afraid to take risks and rely on existing franchises to bring in the dollars. Ryan Coogler made his name with two big budget known IP productions, namely Creed and Black Panther, and now has been given the opportunity to make this very interesting genre-bender. I very much enjoyed Sinners for its compelling story. Coogler really takes the time to establish his main characters and lets the audience get comfortable in the setting. The emphasis on music in the first two acts on the films works really well and the scene in the Juke Joint where Preacherboy performs was heavenly. The drama in this film actually works so well that the genre bend in the third act came as a shock. It was a bold decision and while it could have been a cheap gimmick, it made the film work as a vengeance movie. Spike Lee said he loved this film and I definitely see elements of his work shine through here. Also some nods to masters like Tarantino and Robert Rodriguez. I think the financial succes of Sinners is proof that audiences are still craving original stories on the big screen. Directors should more often be trusted by studios to tell original stories. It does not always work out, but when it does your film becomes part of cinematic history. Sinners is certainly going to be remembered, at the very least by me, a long time from now. MICKEY 17 Although my first Bong was the overall well received Snowpiercer, I have since watched most of his Korean work and found all of them to be more interesting, well crafted films. Bong has a way of making western characters look cartoonish and Mickey 17 is no exception. I found most characters to be obnoxious, even the ones we're supposed to root for, but I don't think that should be attributed to the actors themselves. I also very much disliked the heavy reliance on narration throughout the film and this cuts to my main issue. They failed to convincingly convert the story of Mickey 7 from book to film. This is not a short movie, but it feels rushed nonetheless. I believe more story lines and characters from the novel should have been cut, but even then I would not have liked Mickey 17. Okja and to a lesser degree Snowpiercer suffered from similar problems with people acting and behaving unnaturally, which convinces me that Bong Joon-Ho should simply refrain from making any more Hollywood productions. PAST LIVES I watched this film last year but only now came to write a review about it. Past Lives is a very well crafted drama that cleverly avoids so many possible clichÃ©s it could have trapped itself in. Past Lives is a realistic portrayal of the "one that got away" trope. It was refreshing to see people deal with their relationships and feelings in healthy ways rather than toxic, disorderly ones which seems to be the default in Hollywood. I liked how Hae Sung's love for Nora is never treated with hostility by Arthur, but rather with compassion and respect. People fall in love all the time and it is only natural that you meet more than one person that is a potential life partner. Nora had already settled down with Arthur and while Hae Sung does make her heart skip a beat, is that enough to leave everything behind? Past Lives is a love triangle that never does what you expect it's going to do. The lack of 'drama' has the potential to make for some anti-climactic cinema, but on the contrary, Past Lives' final moments were bittersweet and a strangely cathartic experience for me. I was very much moved by these intelligent adults, making rational, dare I say bourgeois decisions. Perhaps because it is so very relatable. Most people will choose the safe and familiar over the new and exciting and while I am not here to tell you what is right and what is wrong, I think there is beautfy in self control and appreciating what you have. ROMAN HOLIDAY With two of the most handsome people in Hollywood history and Rome, pre-mass tourism, as the third main character, Roman Holiday is eye candy. Yet underneath that sugar coated facade lies a strong, heartfelt production. Audrey Hepburn was a relative unknown before this, but boy was she on fire. She has a very unique composure and combines strength and feminity in a way I have never seen before. I read that she was very fashion conscious and was heavily involved with choosing the outfits for her characters. Gregory Peck, Hepburns strong performing counterpart, was one of the first to realize how big Hepburn was going to be and insisted Paramount put her name next to his on the posters because they would look foolish if they didn't. In hindsight it was the only right decision. While Peck is certainly not overshadowed by Hepburn, she is clearly the star in this evergreen romantic drama. A story I wanted to live in much longer that its runtime allowed me to. A fairytale, but also a story we can all relate to in a way. Going abroad is a great way to discover who you are, or who you would rather be. This makes the ending, where the princess has to decide between her duties and her desires, all the more dramatic. Hepburn's performances in those final scenes are what really sets her apart. With subtle facial expressions she is able to convey so much. Recently I started to enjoy watching older films and Roman Holiday is just one you can't go wrong with. Truly a classic, go see it! THE BRUTALIST The Brutalist is in many ways an homage to the days that I would like to call peak-cinema. From the 50s film directors started to get more creative control, leading to films gradually being recognized as products of art, rather than entertainment. Meanwhile, technological advancements and the introduction of colour television increased pressure on film studios and cinemas to distinguish themselves. This lead to an age of wonderful, big budget epics with longer runtimes and of course to the invention of premium film formats like 70mm Vistavision in which The Brutalist was shot. With its long runtime, interlude, intermission and epilogue, The Brutalist is as close as you can get to the experience of going to the movie theatre in the 50s or 60s. I absolutely loved the visual style of this film. Shooting analogue is the vinyl of movies and I enjoyed the warm, dreamy color palette this film was drenched in. The soundtrack was equally impressive and really set the mood. The acting performances were solid with Guy Pearce being the most notable. Adrien Brody was strong, but his performance reminded me too much of his character in The Pianist. Yet for all its visual force, the story of this film is really nothing we haven't seen or heard before. The plot has been compared to Once Upon a Time in America. The power dynamic between Brody and Pearce reminded me a lot of There Will Be Blood and Adrien Brody's character arc was strangely reminiscent to that of Lawrence of Arabia. Director Corbet certainly did a lot of borrowing and that is fine, but he failed to combine these elements into something entirely new. I try to judge films as a visual medium first and visually The Brutalist is a must-see film. An ode to better days and anyone who shoots analogue in the 21st century deserves a fistbump. Storywise the film was too meager and too blunt to be truly considered the modern classic critics make it out to be. I would rather like to see this project as the starting point of yet another era of peak-cinema. As streaming dominates the film industry, studios once again have to distinguish themselves to draw crowds into cinemas. Shooting and screening films in analogue format might actually be the unique selling point that streaming services could never offer. FLOW Went to see Flow the other day with my kids because it got so much praise by critics. After having experienced it I have mixed feelings. For all it's obvious strengths, this movie certainly has its shortcomings. This film excels as an audiovisual meditation on life, survival, loss and balance. Praise can be given to the interesting animation style, the very realistic animal sounds and movements and the beautiful score. What I liked most about Flow is how it allows animals just be themselves. In most movies featuring animals, they are being given human traits, such as the ability to speak and wearing clothes, in order to be relatable to human audiences. Flow proves that animals can be perfectly relatable just by being themselves. As for the story, Flow started out promising as we follow Cat, the protagonist, being forced out of its habitat by a flood. Cat is a solistic creature, but has to connect to the animals it meets along the way in order to survive as they sail along, looking for a new place to live. The film started to become repetitive somewhere around the middle. Perhaps it's because I've never liked being at sea, but the extended time spent on tiny boats made me feel claustrophobic. Furthermore I think this film lacked direction, leaving the audience to drift along, wondering where it's being taken. Here we see the problem with the dialogue-less style and animals, being themselves, as main characters. The audience is pretty much left to its own devices in deciphering what is going on. I for one was feeling lost at sea near the end. The film also pushed the limits of my concentation with a 90 minute runtime, which frankly is too long for the kind of movie it is. My kids did enjoy the film, especially my three year old was intrigued by it. At that age it must be easier to just live in the moment and go with the flow. ANORA I had my doubts about this film when I saw the trailer, because it looked like a typical romance drama with elements of Pretty Woman and Romeo & Juliet written all over it. However, With Sean Baker (the Florida Project) as the writer, director and editor of the film, I was confident that Anora was going to be something special. Anora's strength lies in it's humanist, realist approach of a story that could have easily fallen into tons of Hollywood clichÃ©s. Watching this film is like starting out in Disneyland, where everything feels like magic, but then slowly walking your way back into the real world. Here class differences are abundant and 'Pretty Woman' fairytales usually don't happen. Mikey Madison did a tremendous job here. At times incredibly fierce but also convincingly vulnerable when she needs to be. An Oscar-worthy performance without a doubt. What really shines through in this film is Sean Baker's humanist approach. Most of his characters have depth and as the story progresses, initial antagonists become vulnerable and even lovable. In the end most people working against Anora and Vanya's relationship are just cogs in the machine of a billionaire, afraid to bite the hand that feeds them. What was suprising is how much Anora is actually a comedy when the trailer sells it more as a romantic drama. During the second act the film goes all in on the comedy, sometimes bordering on slapstick. This is probably also the weakest act of the film. Where the slapstick initially comes as a refreshing suprise, it drags on for at least 10 minutes too long and had me longing for a more mature, cathartic third act. Fortunately the third act delivers with final scene that hit me like a suckerpunch and really shows Baker's talent as a writer and filmmaker. With Anora he has delivered a work that will do well both in mainstream and arthouse theaters. LAWRENCE OF ARABIA Lawrence of Arabia is one of the greatest achievements in the history of cinema. Watching this film in 2024 it is notable how very well this work has stood the test of time. Even with it's runtime of over three hours, the film is able to capture its audience's attention from the beginning and doesn't let go. Director David Lean fell in love with the desert while he was shooting Lawrence of Arabia and his love is enshrined in the wonderful shots you find throughout the film, making the desert feel like an unforgiving, yet magical place. Shooting the film in 70mm helps the audience keep track of the smallest details happening during the grand scenes aginst the backdrop of endless sand dunes. One of the biggest strengths is in the screenplay though. Lawrence of Arabia succeeds in combining a grand story of how the Arabs were tricked by the British into revolting against the Ottoman Empire, with the personal story of Lawrence's transformation and internal struggles as he slowly realises that he is being played by two sides. Now, there are historians who doubt this portrayal of Lawrence and argue that he knew very well that the Arabs would not be getting their independent state, but for the dramatic purposes of this film, a more naive, ideological version of Lawrence helps to make him more likable. Strong, memorable characters can be found throughout the film and the formation of a 'band of brothers' around Lawrence is reminiscent of adventure stories like Seven Samurai and Star Wars. The film goes on to spoil its audience with excellent battle scenes, a majestic score and even a hint at queer love which is probably as far as film studios dared to go in the 60's. Watching this film today, with the ongoing massacre in Palestine, is a stark reminder of the roots of the ongoing instability in the Middle-East. Everything that has happened here in the last century, from the creation of an Arabic national identity, to the crude divisions of the Ottoman Empire after WWI, to the creation of a Jewish State and the ongoing wars over oil have been decisions made by the leaders of Western nations to ultimately protect their own interests at the costs of peace and stability in the Middle-East. INDIANA JONES TRILOGY After having finally watched the Indiana Jones trilogy it is time to give my two cents on which installment is the best one. With all three films fresh in mind I can confidently declare that Raiders of the Lost Ark takes the cake. While Temple of Doom distinguishes itself by being the darker, edgier sequel, seeping into horror at times and the Last Crusade is the most complete, mature Indy film, they are both a step down from Raiders in my opinion. Raiders just rocks in terms of overall atmosphere and the build-up of tension towards the end is very well done. I also liked that Indy is a lot more vulnerable in this film. He really needs his companions Marion and Sallah several times to save his ass. In later films Indy becomes this unbeatable action hero who doesnât really need the people around him to complete his mission. Itâs so disappointing to watch the female lead in Temple of Doom after having enjoyed Marion in Raiders, who is quite empowered. In the making-of documentary Spielberg explains that they wanted a different female lead for each film, but I think they should have just stuck with Marion as she brings a lot of heart to the screen and she wasnât afraid to call out Indy for his bullshit. I also liked that in Raiders, Indy has a clear nemesis in Belloq, who seems to be one step ahead of him every time. In the making-of, Spielberg explains that for Temple of Doom they used a lot of leftover storyboards from Raiders and developed a story around that. This makes Temple of Doom like a B-side album and it certainly feels that way. A lot of cool sequences like the mine cart chase, but the story lacks coherence. The Last Crusade felt like a very safe film that is almost a copy-paste of Raiders. If it wasnât for the father-son dynamic, this movie would have nothing to show for itself. In conclusion: 1. Raiders of the Lost Ark 2. Temple of Doom (Points for the opening sequence in Shanghai, the darker themes and at least the attempt of making something new) 3. Last Crusade (Really just a box office friendly film that hardly adds any new elements to the Indiana Jones universe) CASABLANCA What is the difference between art and craftsmanship? Can one exist without the other? Casablanca is one of those movies that feature on all time best movie lists. That film you have to confess you haven't seen yet with the disclaimer that you do have the vague intention of doing so one day. Last night I finally watched Casablanca after picking it up from a thrift store last week. Casablanca was produced in the middle of World War II. Like so many films in those days it was based on a play and the title was an imitation from the 1938 film Algiers. The director is not one known for it's great artistic vision but rather a studio man. The film, in all honesty, was made because audiences wanted a story about the war and Warner Brothers wanted to cash in on that. Nothing about this film screams art. The film's qualities can mostly be found in how well crafted it is. From the solid acting performances, Ingrid Bergman literally sparkles in this film, to the wonderful set of Rick's Cafe Americain that is so full of life, through to the exceptional use of lighting. The soundtrack with the recurring theme "As Time Goes By" is memorable, as are the many iconic phrases like "Here's looking at you, kid", that left their impact on pop-culture to this day. I believe that art can not exist without craftmanship. Any artist needs to master the craft before they can properly express themselves in it's language. At the same time craftsmanship can elevate a product to artistic heights. I think Casablanca is loved because it falls in this category. A film that stands the test of time because all the people working on the film delivered excellent work, creating a whole that is greater than the sum of it's parts. MEMORIES OF MURDER Bong Joon Ho has a reputation for creating genre movies that follow common structures and tropes of the genre, but then deviating from it, breaking the rules and confusing his audience. Memories of Murder was Bong's second feature film and the first to get international recognition. The story is based on the Hwaseong murders, the first known case of a serial killer in South-Korea. A case that remained unsolved and puzzled a nation for decades (although the killer was finally identified in 2019 through DNA research). What I liked about Memories of Murder is that Bong's genre subversion is more than a gimmick. It serves a purpose for the story he is telling. The detectives being corrupt and incompetent fit within the narrative of the unsolved mystery. Bong's implication being that it may not have been the exceptional skill of the murderer, but rather the incompetence of the protagonists, as the main reason why the killer was never caught. The movie's setting in the 1980's, when South-Korea was a military dictatorship, is also implied as a reason why the case remained unsoled. The police was too busy supressing riots elsewhere in the province to put more people on the case. Meanwhile, the lead detective of the story actively participates in corruption, faking evidence and torturing suspects to get a confession out of them. These detectives do not deserve their happy ending. Although there really is no winner in this case, the detectives inability to solve the case, can be considered justice in the eye of the audience. Memories of Murder is a fascinating work. More rough around the edges than later films like Mother, Snowpiercer and Parasite, but this makes it easier to observe how Bong plays with and defies Hollywood conventions to tell an essentially Korean story. FURIOSA I can not believe that this movie is struggling to make some decent revenue at the box office. Well, actually I can believe it. Most people would rather waste their money on another generic superhero movie. Mad Max has always been kind of a weird niche franchise. Fury Road was a suprise hit 9 years ago, but has reached modern-classic status in just a few years and is considered by many to be one of the greatest action films of all time. I will give you three good reasons why you need to watch this movie before it leaves the theaters. 1. Nobody does action scenes in the 21st century like George Miller. What is especially strong about Furiosa is how he manages to make action scenes feel grand without losing focus. Modern action movies tend to be an overkill of everything, with complex mission objectives making it hard to follow what is going on. Miller always keeps the story simple. For example: A truck loaded with food is being attacked before it can arrive to it's desination. Audiences need a story to hold on to during an action scene, but that story should extremely simple. George Miller understands this and that is why Mad Max's action scenes are leagues better than what you get in most Marvel or DC movies. 2. This may very well be the last Mad Max for the forseeable future. Now that Furiosa looks to be a box office bomb, it is highly unlikely that we're going to see another sequel any time soon. Meanwhile George Miller will turn 80 soon. I think it's not a stretch to assume that Furiosa is going to be the last Mad Max film from the mind of George Miller. Without the creative father of the series I have little hope for anything meaningful being released in the next decades. 3. This movie is a rare breed of a big budget blockbuster film that is actually good. It has a strong creative vision from it's director, lots of memorable characters and great acting performances, some excellent world building and amazing setpieces. CGI is used functionally to enhance scenes and certain moments, but is not over relied upon. The sound effects are powerful and you really need to hear the roaring of the engines with a proper sound system to understand why I'm raving about this picture. CHALLENGERS Challengers was sexy, intense, funny and ultimately disappointing. The acting performances, particularly Zendaya, are strong. The soundtrack was cool and refreshing at first, but overdone near the end. The same goes for the abundance of tennis scenes and the main actors faces in slo-mo close-up throughout the film. That is to say that Challengers plays with a lot of creative audiovisual ideas, but fails to balance this out with a compelling story. There is not enough character development and backstory which makes all the mains look unsympathetic near the end. The film ends up being shallow and you wonder what the take home message was supposed to be. Pro tennis players are all obsessive, power abusing freaks? In spite of what I just said, Challengers was an enjoyable past-time. If only for Zendaya, who really is a shining star in the Hollywood landscape, you will probably have a good time watching this flick. GODZILLA MINUS ONE I love me some Godzilla every now and then. Nothing beats watching a giant atomic lizard pulverizing cities. Godzilla began as a metaphor for the destruction of Japan by nuclear weapons, However, most people just want to watch a great Kaiju flick once in a while. Toho studios, who owns the copyrights to Godzilla, released over 30 Godzilla films over the years. After Godzilla: Final Wars" in 2004 Toho put the franchise on an indefinite hiatus. It was Legendary Pictures with their 2014 "Godzilla" that sparked new life into the series. While we do have Legendary to thank for this, the films have mostly been a major disappointment. Legendary's movies are, even as Kaiju flicks, poorly written. All characters are bland and shallow, storylines are rushed to get to the fighting and motivations are unclear. This makes the expensive, CGI heavy fighting scenes boring to watch because we have no emotional investment in the characters. With Godzilla Minus One, Toho uses it's many years of experience to make a Godzilla film plenty of human drama. The film only cost 10-15 million dollars to make but walked away with the best VFX oscar nonetheless, putting all the major film studios to shame. The truth with any monster movie is, that less is more. We don't actually see Godzilla on screen all that much. It's the anticipation of Godzilla that is truly scary. In Godzilla Minus One, Godzilla's laser beam feels as dangerous as a nuclear weapon and everytime he was about to use it, I was at the edge of my seat. This movie to me felt like Toho saying "Thanks a lot Legendary Pictures, but we'll take it from here." CIVIL WAR Civil War is an impressive work that confronts western audiences with what we believe could never happen here. Recent polarization in the west and the january 6th Capitol riots have somewhat woken people up. Peace can be easily disrupted under the right circumstances. The acting performances of all the mains are solid and I particularly liked Cailee Spaeny as the reckless rookie warphotographer. Jesse Plemons appears in only one scene in the movie, but his performance was hauntingly good and by far the most memorable scene. I used to call him evil Matt Damon but he has become his own phenomenon at this point. For all that I enjoyed about Civil War, I still felt slightly disappointed because this film is only a few notches away from being a classic, but the scenario and writing is a bit immature at times. I liked how this movie explores the relationship between Dunst and Spaeny, but I wish they'd focus more on this aspect. Also, the notion that war journalists are all restless adrenaline seekers sounds simplistic. In conclusion, Civil War is a wake up call and an entertaining, intelligent action movie. MONKEY MAN To describe Dev Patel's directorial debut as 'Indian John Wick' would on the one hand be lazy, but on the other hand pretty accurate. Patel is not blind to the resemblances either and directly references John Wick in the movie at some point. If anything, Monkey Man is a more intense, more violent and more down to earth version of the very popular franchise that has been gradually losing significance since the third installment. Where John Wick started as a no nonsense revenge movie, the sequels started to bore the audience with a lot of self-referential crap and lore that the audience could do without. Monkey Man is refreshing in that regard. Patel's debut is vibrant, intense and rough around the edges. The characters have clear goals and motivations and fighting scenes, though sometimes overly curel and gorey, serve a purpose. It's worth mentioning that Dev Patel, in the tradition of John Wick and martial arts legends before him, does all the fighting in the movie himself. This alone makes Monkey Man a recommended watch! Update: For a more comprehensive review of Monkey Man I'd like to redirect you to Saikyo Central who wrote an excellent, insightful piece. THE HOLDOVERS Alexander Payne's latest feature film gained five Oscar nominations and won one. While it certainly had it's moments, my overall experience was somewhat disappointing. The main characters all have interesting story arcs but the overall story lacked urgency. The film is also a bit too long and feels unfocused at times. The acting performances were strong and Da'Vine Joy Randolph's performance felt sincere, but to me was not outstanding enough to be Oscar worthy. That being said The Holdovers is an enjoyable watch that is well written and Paul Giamatti is excellent as the grumpy, sadistic history teacher. Alexander Payne's films are often like that. Well written and enjoyable in the moment, but not very memorable. His storytelling is getting repetitive. In that regard the Oscar nomations perhaps elevated my expectations too high. DUNE PART TWO Villeneuve has proven to be able to create a movie that is visually breathtaking, but also stimulating intellectually. Dune's setpieces have this way of making the audience feel tiny and fragile in the unforgiving landscape of Arrakis. The cast is on fire and I was cheering for cute couple Muad'dib and Chani the entire three hours. But the greatest triumph is the soundtrack and sound effects. Sound plays an important role in the Dune films, summoning the Shai'hulud is a thrill everytime and the scene where Paul tries to ride one was amazing. Also compliments to Hans Zimmer who captures the atmosphere of Dune so well. Dune Part One and Two are easily the most impressive films I have seen in the cinema in the past ten years. IO CAPITANO An impressive production from the director of Gomorra. Io Capitano sheds light on a world that as a European I hear about daily on the news, yet seems to be so far away from me. The journey of labour migrants seeking a better life in Europe is terrifying. What shocked me the most is how the constant flow of refugees has created systems along migration routes where people are exploited and abused systematically for profit. It is then quite impressive how Mateo Garrone is able to create a balanced film that mixes light, wholesome moments with the very likeable main characters, with tragic and shocking scenes that show the grim reality behind the refugee/labour migrant crisis we face in Europe. // Home // About // Blog // Old Net Stories // Sozai Museum // Writings // Film Reviews // MIDI-hall // Scans // Links // Collections //
